title: First commands & files
objective: The very first commands: check the system, make files and folders, and move around.

questions.q: Which command shows which Red Hat version your machine is running?
questions.explain: `/etc/redhat-release` is a small text file holding the OS version; `cat` prints it.

questions.q: What does `whoami` print?
options: The username you are currently logged in as
questions.explain: It answers "who am I right now" — useful when you switch users later.

questions.q: What does `touch linux{1..50}.txt` create?
options: 50 files named linux1.txt through linux50.txt in one command
questions.explain: `{1..50}` is brace expansion — bash expands it to 1 2 3 … 50 before touch runs.

questions.q: What is wrong with `mkdir mydata1 mydata 2 mydata3`?
options: The space in "mydata 2" makes mkdir create two folders: "mydata" and "2"
mkdir cannot make more than one folder
questions.explain: Spaces separate arguments, so `mydata 2` is read as two names. Write `mydata2` with no space.

questions.q: What does `cd ..` do?
options: Moves up one level to the parent directory
questions.explain: `..` means "parent". `cd ~` (or just `cd`) goes home; `cd /` goes to the root.

questions.q: Linux is case-sensitive. Why did `cd desktop` fail but `cd Desktop` work?
options: The folder is named "Desktop" with a capital D, and Linux treats names case-sensitively
questions.explain: `Desktop` and `desktop` are different names on Linux.

questions.q: Create an empty file called myfile.txt.
questions.explain: `touch` makes a new empty file (or updates the time on an existing one).

questions.q: Create three files at once named myfile.doc, myfile.pdf and myfile.html.
questions.explain: `touch` accepts several names separated by spaces.

questions.q: Make 50 folders named linux51 through linux100 in one command.
questions.explain: Brace expansion works for mkdir too.

questions.q: Print the full path of the directory you are standing in.
questions.explain: "print working directory".

questions.q: Go back to your home directory from anywhere.
questions.explain: `cd` with no argument, or `cd ~`, returns home.

labs.title: Your first files and folders
labs.scenario: Check your Red Hat version and who you are, make a folder "mydata", create files linux1.txt to linux50.txt, then make folders linux51 to linux100.

labs.title: Navigation practice
labs.scenario: From your home directory, go into Desktop, list it, come back up, go into Downloads, then return home. Watch the prompt and pwd at each step.

title: cat and echo: creating and filling files
objective: Use cat and echo to create files, write into them, and append.

questions.q: What does `cat linux10.txt` do?
options: Prints the contents of linux10.txt on the screen
questions.explain: `cat` shows a file's contents.

questions.q: What does `cat > linux10.txt` do?
options: Creates (or overwrites) the file and lets you type its contents; press Ctrl+D to finish
questions.explain: `>` redirects what you type into the file, replacing anything already there.

questions.q: What is the difference between `cat > file` and `cat >> file`?
options: `>` overwrites the file; `>>` adds to the end (appends)
questions.explain: One arrow replaces, two arrows append — the same rule applies to `echo`.

questions.q: What does `echo welcome to jspm > linux1.txt` do?
options: Writes the text "welcome to jspm" into linux1.txt, overwriting it
Prints the text on screen only
questions.explain: `echo` prints text; `>` sends that text into the file instead of the screen.

questions.q:
`echo -e "i
am
root"` — what does `-e` and `
` do?
options: -e enables escape sequences, and \n inserts a new line
questions.explain: With `-e`, `\n` = newline, `\t` = tab, `\b` = backspace, `\v` = vertical tab.

questions.q: Why does `echo"hello"` fail but `echo "hello"` work?
options: A space is needed between the command "echo" and its argument
questions.explain: The shell needs a space to separate the command from what you give it.

questions.q: Print the file linux1.txt to the screen.
questions.explain: `cat` dumps the whole file.

questions.q: Create the file linux10.txt and type its contents from the keyboard (overwriting it).
questions.explain: Finish typing with Ctrl+D.

questions.q: Add more lines to the end of linux10.txt from the keyboard.
questions.explain: `>>` keeps the existing contents and appends.

questions.q: Write "welcome to rscoe" to the end of linux1.txt without erasing it.
questions.explain: `>>` appends; `>` would overwrite.

questions.q: Print three words on three separate lines using echo with escapes.
questions.explain: `-e` turns on `\n` as a newline.

labs.title: Overwrite vs append
labs.scenario: Create linux1.txt with "hii i am pranjal", view it, then append "welcome to rscoe", view it again, then overwrite it with "hii i am linux user".
steps: echo hii i am pranjal > linux1.txt
echo hii i am linux user > linux1.txt

labs.title: Escape sequences
labs.scenario: Use echo -e to write text with newlines into a file called linuxg.txt, then view it.
steps:
echo -e "i
am
root for this
linux class only" > linuxg.txt

title: date and cal
objective: Read and format the date, and print calendars.

questions.q: What does `date` with no options print?
questions.explain: Add a `+format` to show only the parts you want.

questions.q: What does `date +%B` show?
questions.explain: `%b` is the short month name (Oct), `%B` the full one (October).

questions.q: Which format code gives the 4-digit year?
questions.explain: `%Y` = 2026, `%y` = 26 (two digits), `%m` = month number, `%d` = day of month.

questions.q: What does `cal 2026` display?
options: The full calendar for the whole year 2026
questions.explain: `cal` alone shows this month; a year number shows all 12 months.

questions.q: What does `cal -j` show?
options: A calendar with Julian day numbers (day-of-year, 1–365)
questions.explain: `-j` numbers each day by its position in the year.

questions.q: How do you read the manual for the date command?
questions.explain: `man date` opens the manual; `cal --help` gives a quick option summary.

questions.q: Show today's day-of-month number only.
questions.explain: `%d` is the numeric day (01–31).

questions.q: Show the full month name of today.
questions.explain: `%B` = full month name.

questions.q: Show the 4-digit year.
questions.explain: `%Y` is the four-digit year.

questions.q: Print this month's calendar.
questions.explain: `cal` alone shows the current month.

questions.q: Print the calendar for the whole year 2026.
questions.explain: A year argument prints all 12 months.

labs.title: Date formatting drill
labs.scenario: Print, each on its own line: the day number, the month number, the short month name, the full month name, and the four-digit year.

labs.title: Calendars
labs.scenario: Show this month, then the whole of 2026, then a calendar with Julian (day-of-year) numbers. Read the manual for cal.

title: Exploring the filesystem
objective: Move through the Linux directory tree and read system files.

questions.q: On Linux, everything lives under which single top directory?
questions.explain: There are no drive letters; `/` is the root of the whole tree.

questions.q: Which directory holds system configuration files like /etc/passwd?
questions.explain: `/etc` = configuration. `/bin` and `/usr/bin` hold programs, `/var/log` holds logs.

questions.q: What does /etc/passwd contain?
options: One line per user account with fields separated by colons
questions.explain: The password itself is not here (it shows as `x`); it's the account list.

questions.q: What is the difference between `ls -l` and `ls -ld` on a folder?
options: `ls -l` lists what's inside the folder; `ls -ld` shows the folder's own details
questions.explain: `-ld` is how you check a directory's own permissions and owner.

questions.q: Why does `cd..` (no space) fail while `cd ..` works?
options: A space is required between the command and its argument
questions.explain: `cd` is the command, `..` is the argument — they must be separated by a space.

questions.q: Which command recalls the commands you have typed before?
questions.explain: `history` lists them; you can also search with Ctrl+R.

questions.q: Go to the root of the filesystem.
questions.explain: A single `/` is the top of the tree.

questions.q: Print the account list file.
questions.explain: Each line is one account.

questions.q: Show the details (permissions, owner) of the folder mydata itself, not its contents.
questions.explain: `-d` means "the directory itself".

questions.q: Show your command history.
questions.explain: Numbers let you rerun with `!number`.

labs.title: A tour of the tree
labs.scenario: Starting from /, visit and list these directories, noticing what each holds: /etc, /bin, /var/log, /usr/bin, /tmp. Return home afterward.

labs.title: Read system files
labs.scenario: Look at the Red Hat version, the account list, and the long listing of /etc.

title: Searching text with grep
objective: Find lines that match a pattern, and change what grep reports.

questions.q: What does `grep root /etc/passwd` do?
options: Prints every line of /etc/passwd that contains "root"
questions.explain: `grep PATTERN FILE` prints matching lines.

questions.q: What does `grep -n` add to the output?
options: The line number of each match
questions.explain: `-n` prefixes each matching line with its number.

questions.q: What does `grep -v pranjal passwd` show?
options: Every line that does NOT contain "pranjal"
questions.explain: `-v` inverts the match.

questions.q: What does `grep -o pranjal passwd` print?
options: Only the matched word "pranjal" from each match, not the whole line
questions.explain: `-o` shows only the matching part.

questions.q: What does `grep -e prasanna -e pranjal passwd` do?
questions.explain: Each `-e` adds another pattern to search for.

questions.q: How do you see all the options grep supports quickly?
questions.explain: `grep --help` prints a summary; `man grep` is the full manual.

questions.q: Show the lines of /etc/passwd that contain "root".
questions.explain: Classic way to find the root account's line.

questions.q: Show matching lines with their line numbers for the word "passwd" in the file tmp.
questions.explain: `-n` adds line numbers.

questions.q: Show the lines of tmp that do NOT contain "pranjal".
questions.explain: `-v` inverts the match.

questions.q: Print only the matched word (with line numbers) for "pranjal" in tmp.
questions.explain: `-o` only the match, `-n` line numbers — options can be combined.

labs.title: grep on the account file
labs.scenario: Copy /etc/passwd to a file called tmp, then: find lines with "root", find lines with numbers, show lines without "nologin", and print only the word "bash" where it appears.

labs.title: Two patterns at once
labs.scenario: In tmp, find any line containing either "root" or "bash", with line numbers.

title: sed, cut, sort and counting
objective: Transform and summarise text: substitute, extract columns, sort, and count.

questions.q: What does `sed "s/pranjal/pranju/" tmp` do?
options: Prints tmp with the first "pranjal" on each line replaced by "pranju" (file unchanged)
questions.explain: `s/old/new/` substitutes; add `g` to replace every match on a line.

questions.q: What makes sed change the file itself?
options: Nothing; sed always edits the file
questions.explain: Without `-i`, sed only prints the result and leaves the file as it was.

questions.q: What does `sed '5,7s/purva/pranjal/g' file` do?
options: On lines 5 to 7 only, replaces every "purva" with "pranjal"
questions.explain: `5,7` is a line range; `$` means the last line (e.g. `7,$`).

questions.q: What does `cut -d: -f1 tmp` print?
options: The first field of each line, using ":" as the separator
questions.explain: `-d` sets the delimiter, `-f` picks the field number. `/etc/passwd` uses `:`.

questions.q: What does `sort -n` do that plain `sort` does not?
questions.explain: `-r` reverses, `-t:` sets a field separator, `-k4` sorts by the 4th field.

questions.q: Which counts the number of LINES in a file?
questions.explain: `-l` lines, `-w` words, `-c` characters/bytes.

questions.q: Replace "bin" with "bbin" throughout the file tmp, changing the file itself.
questions.explain: `-i` edits in place; add `g` to catch more than one per line.

questions.q: Print only the first colon-separated field of tmp.
questions.explain: The username field in /etc/passwd.

questions.q: Sort the file tmp in reverse order.
questions.explain: `-r` = reverse.

questions.q: Count how many lines are in tmp.
questions.explain: One line per account, so this also counts accounts.

questions.q: Show the first 2 lines of tmp.
questions.explain: `head` shows the top; `tail` shows the bottom (`tail -6` = last 6).

labs.title: Transform the account file
labs.scenario: Using your tmp copy of /etc/passwd: substitute "nologin" with "lllog" (preview only), then pull out the username column, then sort it, and finally count the lines.

labs.title: Sorting by a field
labs.scenario: Sort tmp by the 3rd field (the UID) numerically, using ":" as the separator.

labs.title: head, tail and wc
labs.scenario: Show the first 7 lines, the last 6 lines, and the line, word and character counts of tmp.

title: Users and groups
objective: Create and modify user accounts and groups.

questions.q: Which command creates a new group called linux?
questions.explain: `groupadd` makes a group; `useradd` makes a user.

questions.q: After `useradd myuser1`, how do you set its password?
questions.explain: `passwd NAME` (as root) sets another user's password.

questions.q: What does `id user2` show?
options: The user's UID, primary group (GID) and supplementary groups
questions.explain: `id` is how you check an account's identity and group memberships.

questions.q: What is the key difference between `usermod -G` and `usermod -aG`?
options: -G replaces all supplementary groups; -aG appends without removing the others
questions.explain: Always use `-aG` to add a group safely — `-G` alone wipes the existing list.

questions.q: What does `usermod -g class user2` change?
questions.explain: Lowercase `-g` = primary group; uppercase `-G` = supplementary groups.

questions.q: What does a shell of /sbin/nologin do for an account?
options: Prevents that account from logging in interactively (used for service accounts)
questions.explain: Set it with `usermod -s /sbin/nologin name` or `useradd -s /sbin/nologin name`.

questions.q: Create a group named linux.
questions.explain: Verify with `cat /etc/group`.

questions.q: Create a user called ram with UID 1089.
questions.explain: `-u` sets the UID; check with `id ram`.

questions.q: Add the user ram to the group kkk WITHOUT removing his other groups.
questions.explain: `-aG` appends; forgetting `-a` would replace all his supplementary groups.

questions.q: Set ram's primary group to class.
questions.explain: Lowercase `-g` for the primary group.

questions.q: Create a user varsha with UID 1095, primary group 2076, and a no-login shell.
questions.explain: Combine options in one useradd command.

questions.q: Set a comment (full name) of "developer2" on the user john_toddler.
questions.explain: `-c` sets the comment/GECOS field; see it in /etc/passwd.

labs.title: Create users and groups
labs.scenario: Create group "linux". Create users prann and user1, both in group linux. Create user2, then change its primary group to a new group "class". Check each with id.

labs.title: Append vs replace groups (the -aG lesson)
labs.scenario: Create user ram. Add him to group kkk, then also to class, then also to linux — all without losing the earlier groups. Then check his groups.

labs.title: One-line account spec
labs.scenario: Create user varsha with UID 1095, primary group 2076 (create the group first), and shell /sbin/nologin. Confirm.

title: Permissions and ownership
objective: Change who owns files and what each class of user may do.

questions.q: In `ls -ld` output like `drwxr-x---`, what are the three groups of rwx for?
questions.explain: Each group is read(r) write(w) execute(x) for that class of user.

questions.q: What does `chmod o+w /mydata` do?
questions.explain: Symbolic mode: who (u/g/o/a), operator (+/-/=), permission (r/w/x).

questions.q: What is the difference between `chmod o=rwx` and `chmod o+rwx`?
options: `=` sets others to exactly rwx; `+` adds rwx to whatever others already have
questions.explain: `=` is absolute, `+`/`-` are relative.

questions.q: What does `chmod 771` mean in numbers?
options: rwx for owner (7), rwx for group (7), execute-only for others (1)

questions.q: What does `chmod g+s` on a directory do (the SGID bit)?
options: New files created inside inherit the directory's group — good for shared folders
questions.explain: You saw this on /data/impdata so a team shares the group automatically.

questions.q: `ls -l /usr/bin/passwd` shows an `s` where owner-execute should be. What is that?
options: The SUID bit: passwd runs with its owner's (root's) privileges so you can change your password
questions.explain: SUID lets a normal user update /etc/shadow safely through passwd.

questions.q: Make myuser the owner of the folder /unnati.
questions.explain: `chown USER path` changes the owner (root only).

questions.q: Change the group of /unnati to sales.
questions.explain: `chgrp` changes just the group (or `chown :sales /unnati`).

questions.q: Give others exactly read, write and execute on /unnati.
questions.explain: `=` sets exactly those permissions for "others".

questions.q: Set /test/impdata to rwx for owner and group, execute-only for others, using numbers.
Turn on the SGID bit on /data/impdata so new files inherit its group.
questions.explain: Or `chmod 2771` (the leading 2 is SGID).

labs.title: Owner, group and permissions
labs.scenario: Create /unnati. Make "myuser" the owner and "sales" the group. Give the owner read+execute, the group rwx, and others nothing. Check with ls -ld after each change.

labs.title: A shared team directory (SGID)
labs.scenario: Create /data/impdata. Make "amit" the owner and "redhat" the group, set mode 771, then add the SGID bit so files made inside belong to the redhat group.

labs.title: See SUID in action
labs.scenario: Look at the permissions of the passwd program and explain why a normal user can change their own password.
steps: # the 's' in the owner slot = SUID: it runs as root (its owner)

title: Switching users and sudo
objective: Become another user, and grant admin rights with wheel and sudo.

questions.q: What is the difference between `su user1` and `su - user1`?
options: `su -` loads user1's full environment and home directory (a login shell); `su` keeps your current environment
`su -` does not ask for a password
questions.explain: Prefer `su -` so the environment matches the target user.

questions.q: When you run `su user1` as a normal user, whose password is asked?
questions.explain: `su` asks for the target user's password; `sudo` asks for your own.

questions.q: On RHEL, members of which group get sudo (admin) rights by default?
questions.explain: Add a user with `usermod -aG wheel name`. The rule is in /etc/sudoers.

questions.q: What is the safe way to edit the sudoers file?
options: visudo (it checks the syntax before saving)
questions.explain: A syntax error in sudoers can lock everyone out of sudo; visudo prevents that.

questions.q: A sudoers rule `user1 ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL,!/usr/bin/passwd` means user1 can:
options: Run any command as root without a password, EXCEPT the passwd command (the ! excludes it)
questions.explain: The `!` negates a command, carving an exception out of "ALL".

questions.q: Switch to the user deep with a full login shell.
questions.explain: The dash gives deep's environment and home directory.

questions.q: Add the user deep to the wheel group so he can use sudo.
questions.explain: `-aG` appends wheel without removing deep's other groups.

questions.q: Safely open the sudoers file for editing.
questions.explain: Always use visudo, never edit /etc/sudoers directly.

labs.title: Become another user
labs.scenario: Create user vilas, give him a bash shell, then switch into his account with a full login shell and check who you are.

labs.title: Grant sudo via wheel
labs.scenario: Create user deep, add him to the wheel group, switch to him, and confirm he can run an admin command with sudo.

labs.title: A custom sudo rule
labs.scenario: Using visudo, let user1 run all commands as root without a password except changing passwords, then test it.
